title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks & Ops Runbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference architecture, kernel scheduling policy, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks for Redwood’s inference serving runtime. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, infra, and SRE teams and for cross-team reviewers during rollouts.

Sections included: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbook (how to run and interpret profiles), benchmarking suite (workloads and expected baselines), release notes summary, known issues and mitigations, and step-by-step runbooks for common incidents.

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

Intro: The serving runtime is a horizontally-scalable, GPU-optimized inference engine that supports model variants, KV cache management, continuous batching, and quantization-friendly execution paths. The runtime exposes a uniform API to higher layers (control plane, routing, and customer-facing APIs) and provides instrumentation for cost and latency accounting.

Components:
- Frontend (api-gateway): handles authentication, request validation, routing, rate limiting, and quick-path fallbacks.
- Router/Dispatcher: enforces routing policies (latency, cost, region, customer tier) and selects target model variant and pool.
- Worker Daemon (runtime-worker): manages model artifacts, kernel selection, dispatcher loop, batching, and KV cache. Each worker runs a single model family variant by default.
- Scheduler (kernel-scheduler): orchestrates GPU slots, quantization kernels, and preemption policies for multi-tenant pools.
- Telemetry and Tracing: emits token-level latency, per-request timeline, GPU utilization, memory high-water marks, and kernel-level timings.
- Caching Layer: prefix/KV cache service for cross-request reuse and persistent in-memory caches on worker nodes.
- Control Plane: model catalogue, versioning, rollout policies, and autoscaling.

Architecture diagram (textual):
- api-gateway -> router -> pool-proxy -> worker (runtime) -> kernel (CUDA/Triton/custom-kernels)
- Telemetry: Each arrow annotated with metrics: request_size, req_enqueue_ms, batch_wait_ms, inference_ms, kernel_ms, p99/p50 latency.

Ownership and SLAs:
- Service owner: serving-runtime team
- SLOs: 99th percentile request latency <= 300ms for small models (<2B) on hosted tier; 99th <= 700ms for medium models (2B-70B) depending on config.
- Error budget and alerting: see Runbook -> Alerts section.

2) Kernel scheduling design and policy

Goals: Ensure predictable latency SLOs, maximize GPU throughput, and minimize OOMs and tail-latency due to contention.

Key concepts:
- Slot: an allocation of GPU memory/compute budget for a worker to accept new batches.
- Kernel profile: precomputed resource usage (VRAM, peak FLOPs, workspace) per model variant and sequence-length bucket.
- Preemption window: configured grace period to evict/bounce low-priority work when higher-priority requests arrive.

Policies:
1. Priority buckets: real-time (hosted API, low-latency customers), reserved (dedicated capacity), background (batch jobs, evals). Higher buckets can preempt lower ones within preemption window.
2. Slot packing: small-token requests are packed into shared slot instances up to safe concurrency based on kernels’ concurrent-exec profile.
3. Kernel selection: the scheduler chooses quantized kernels where available unless disabled by request-level quality flags. Kernel selection considers batch-size, seq_len, and memory headroom.
4. OOM backpressure: if worker memory usage > 85% of GPU memory, scheduler stops accepting new slots and signals autoscaler and router for spillover.

Example scheduling parameters (table):
| Parameter | Default | Notes |
|-----------|---------|-------|
| slot_mem_reserve | 8GB | Per-slot memory reservation baseline for large models |
| preemption_window_ms | 250 | Time to wait before evicting background work |
| max_shared_concurrency | 4 | Max in-slot concurrent stream executions for small kernels |
| oom_hwm_pct | 85 | GPU memory high-water mark to trigger backpressure |

3) Profiling playbook (how to run, interpret, and act)

Overview: Profiling is split into three scopes: micro (kernel-level), infra (GPU/PCIe), and request-level (end-to-end). Use the profiling harness in the benchmarking suite.

Pre-requisites:
- SSH access to worker node or run through infra-proxy
- Profiling toolchain: nvprof/nsight, cupy/pytorch profiling toggles, custom kernel timing hooks (available at /opt/runtime/tools/prof).

Steps:
1. Reproduce load shape locally or in staging. Capture representative traces (at least 5 minutes, 99th percentile traffic).
2. Enable distributed tracing: set X-Trace=1 on requests or use trace sampling via control-plane route.
3. Run kernel sampling: sudo /opt/runtime/tools/profile-kernels.sh --model <model-name> --seq 512 --batch 1,4,8 --mode nvprof
4. Collect GPU metrics: nvidia-smi dmon, nvprof timeline, and device counters for SM utilization, memory throughput, and PCIe.
5. Generate flamegraphs and kernel timelines: /opt/runtime/tools/trace-to-flame.sh <trace.json> -> flame.svg

Interpretation checklist:
- If kernel_ms dominates inference_ms and SM util < 50%: check kernel implementation and fallback kernels.
- If batch_wait_ms large: adjust batching window and batcher policy.
- If CUDA memcopy dominates time: investigate host<->device streaming, use pinned memory or asynchronous copies.
- If p99 dominated by cold-starts: confirm model warm-up and KV cache priming settings.

Actions:
- Update kernel selection table for this model variant and add quantized kernel build if gaps exist.
- Tune scheduler parameters: reduce preemption_window or increase max_shared_concurrency for small kernels.
- Add workload-specific warm-up routines to router.

4) Benchmarking suite and expected baselines

Purpose: Reproducible performance benchmarks for regression detection and capacity planning. Bench harness located at: git.redwood/internal/infra/serving-bench.

Standard workloads (examples):
- micro-latency: 1 request/sec, single-token prompt, measure cold/warm start p50/p95/p99.
- chat-multi-turn: variable sequence up to 1024 tokens, streaming enabled.
- high-throughput: synthetic batch generator with 16 concurrent clients, average seq_len 64, target throughput 5k tokens/sec per GPU.
- embed-bulk: bulk embedding pipeline to measure batching efficiency.

CLI examples:
```
# Run a latency benchmark against staging pool
serving-bench run --pool staging-small --model redwood/gpt-3x-6B-q4f16 --workload micro-latency --concurrency 64 --duration 300
```

Benchmark metrics to record: p50/p95/p99 latencies (ms), tokens/sec, tokens/cost-unit, GPU utilization %, batch occupancy %, kernel_ms distribution, memory_headroom at percentiles.

Expected baseline (example):
- Model: redwood/gpt-3x-6B-q4f16 on A100-80GB
- micro-latency p50: 42ms, p95: 110ms, p99: 180ms when warmed (after 60s warm-up); tokens/sec 4200; GPU util 68%.

Storing results: Bench outputs are saved to performance-bench-db (internal). Each run must include tags: model, kernel-commit, driver-version, cuda-version, hw-type, pool-config.

5) Release notes (recent changes, 2029-04-01 -> 2029-04-10)

2029-04-05: Kernel selection optimizer v1.4 deployed to staging. Changes: improved quantized GEMM code path for seq_len < 128, reduced kernel_ms by ~18% on small prompt workloads.

2029-04-08: Scheduler preemption refinements: preemption_window_ms reduced from 400ms -> 250ms; slot_mem_reserve default lowered from 10GB -> 8GB for improved density on 80GB GPUs.

2029-04-10: Telemetry: added kernel-level histograms to request traces and introduced tokens/cost-unit metric.

Backports: See related_pages for release branches and PR links.

6) Known issues and current mitigations

Issue: p99 spikes on medium models (7B) under multi-tenant load when background evals run.
- Symptom: p99 latency increases by 2-4x during background eval windows.
- Root cause: scheduler allowed background tasks to occupy slots without respecting reserved headroom.
- Mitigation: temporarily reduce background concurrency, increase oom_hwm_pct safeguard, apply preemption policy.
- Planned fix: scheduler patch v1.15 to enforce strict reserved_headroom per pool (ETA 2029-04-18).

Issue: Intermittent OOM during model warmup for quantized kernels.
- Symptom: worker OOM during first warmup on some drivers.
- Workaround: pre-warm models using pre-warm job or disable aggressive workspace allocation for warmup.

Issue: Benchmark noise on older driver versions causing inconsistent kernel timings.
- Workaround: pin driver version for benchmark-run tags and only compare runs with identical driver/cuda tags.

7) Runtime runbooks (step-by-step)

Alert: High p99 latency (hosted)
1. Identify impacted pool: dash -> serving-runtime -> p99 latency by pool.
2. Check worker-level traces for batch_wait_ms and kernel_ms.
3. If batch_wait_ms >> kernel_ms: increase worker replicas or adjust batch-window-ms via /api/admin/pool/<pool>/config.
4. If kernel_ms dominant and SM util low: capture kernel profile; route traffic to fallback kernel variant (via control plane) and open ticket for kernel team.
5. If OOMs observed: mark pool ReadOnly in router, drain new requests, escalate to infra-sre.
6. Post-incident: run perf-bench to confirm remediation, update incident review.

Alert: GPU OOM on worker
1. Check dmesg, /var/log/runtime/oom.log, and telemetry for memory high-water percentiles.
2. If warmup caused OOM: restart worker with model_warmup_enabled=false and schedule prewarm job on another node.
3. Increase slot_mem_reserve or reduce max_batch_size for problematic model as short-term fix.
4. If repeated across nodes: escalate to infra-sre and mark possible driver issue.

Alert: High error rate for a model variant (500s)
1. Fetch latest logs: /opt/runtime/logs/<worker-id>.log and request traces.
2. If serialization or model load errors: check model artifact checksum and re-pull artifact from control plane.
3. If kernel crashes: isolate to kernel commit and roll back to previous kernel-commit via control plane.

8) Team wiki and operating practices

Essential links (team wiki):
- Kernel builds: git.redwood/internal/infra/kernel-builds
- Benchmark harness: git.redwood/internal/infra/serving-bench
- Telemetry schema: git.redwood/internal/infra/telemetry/schema.md
- Incident board: jira.redwood/browse/SERVRUNTIME

Best practices:
- Always run the standard benchmark suite after a kernel or scheduler change and tag runs.
- Include kernel-commit, driver-version, and hw-type in all perf PRs.
- For model onboarding, attach profiling artifacts and warm-up plan to the model PR.

9) Appendix: example configs and CLI snippets

A. Sample scheduler config (YAML):
```
scheduler:
  slot_mem_reserve: 8GB
  preemption_window_ms: 250
  max_shared_concurrency: 4
  oom_hwm_pct: 85
  reserved_headroom_pct: 10
```

B. Sample telemetry fragment (JSON):
```
{
  "request_id": "abc123",
  "model_variant": "redwood/gpt-3x-6B-q4f16",
  "kernel_ms": 34.2,
  "batch_wait_ms": 12.6,
  "gpu_util_pct": 68.0
}
```

C. Useful CLI:
```
# Profile kernels for model
sudo /opt/runtime/tools/profile-kernels.sh --model redwood/gpt-3x-6B-q4f16 --seq 512 --batch 8 --mode nvprof
# Run benchmark
serving-bench run --pool staging --model redwood/gpt-3x-6B-q4f16 --workload high-throughput --duration 600
# Toggle route warmup
curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' https://controlplane.internal/api/pool/staging/config -d '{"warmup_enabled": true}'
```

10) Post-incident and maintenance checklist

- Document the incident with timeline and root cause in confluence and link to this page.
- If changes to scheduler or kernel are required, include benchmark PR with before/after data.
- Add regression tests to the benchmark suite for the observed workload.
- Schedule a follow-up: owner must present findings in the next weekly runtime sync.

Contact matrix:
- Serving runtime owners: runtime-team@redwood.internal (on-call rota in pagerduty)
- Kernel engineering: kernels@redwood.internal
- Infra SRE: infra-sre@redwood.internal

Notes and future work:
- Plan to introduce per-request QoS tokens to reduce preemption churn.
- Investigate tighter integration with cloud provider’s MIG features for small-model density.
- Tracking: scheduler v1.15 to land 2029-04-18 with reserved_headroom enforcement.
